summary: Defines an experimental change to TLS to support the certificate types specified by IEEE and ETSI, used by Intelligent Transport Systems such as connected vehicles, to authenticate TLS entities.

eli5.summary: Cars and roadside gear have their own kinds of ID cards. This document teaches the secure-connection system to understand those cards so such devices can prove who they are.

subtitle: Adding ITS vehicle certificates to TLS secure connections

tldr.problem: Intelligent Transport Systems (ITS) such as connected vehicles use compact, specialized certificates from IEEE and ETSI that carry embedded permission information, but the TLS protocol only recognized X.509 certificates and raw public keys.
tldr.mechanism: This document extends TLS 1.3 to negotiate and use ITS certificates via new certificate type extensions, allowing both clients and servers to authenticate using these vehicle-specific certificates while maintaining backward compatibility.
tldr.outcome: ITS systems can now establish secure TLS connections using their native certificate format, enabling direct authentication in vehicular networks, V2X deployments, and roadside infrastructure across Europe and the United States.

today: RFC 8902 is Experimental and not an Internet Standard Track specification. It enables a real, deployed authentication method for vehicular networks. The extension is in use across Europe, North America, and Australia in ITS deployments, and automakers have committed to supporting it in new vehicles.

sections.title: ITS Certificates and Why They Matter
sections.content:
ITS certificates are certificate types defined by IEEE Standard 1609.2 and ETSI TS 103097 for vehicular communications. Unlike X.509 certificates, ITS certificates are optimized for bandwidth and latency in vehicular ad hoc networks: they are more compact and carry embedded authorization permissions (appPermissions field) so a receiver can make an instant allow/deny decision without consulting a remote server.

The compact format is critical in ITS: vehicular networks often operate on 10 MHz channels with 6 Mbps throughput, and vehicles need to authenticate roadside units and other vehicles within 300-500 meters with minimal delay. ITS certificates carry a PSID (ITS Application Identifier) and optional SSP (Service Specific Permissions) that define what activities the certificate holder can perform.

The EU has committed to ITS certificate use in Cooperative Intelligent Transport Systems, automakers including Volkswagen and GM have deployed V2X using ITS certificates, and the US DOT has proposed regulations requiring ITS support in all light vehicles. This RFC enables TLS itself to work with these native certificate types rather than requiring conversion to X.509.
sections.eli5: Vehicles use their own kind of ID card that is smaller and says what they can do. TLS is the system that makes secure connections. This section explains why TLS needs to understand vehicle IDs so cars can talk securely.

sections.title: Certificate Type Extension in TLS 1.3
sections.content:
The extension follows RFC 7250 procedures and uses the client_certificate_type and server_certificate_type extensions to negotiate which certificate type will be used. A new certificate type, 1609Dot2 (value 3), is added to the CertificateType enumeration alongside the existing X509 (value 0) and RawPublicKey (value 2).

Unlike earlier TLS versions, the client and server can independently choose different certificate types: the client might send an ITS certificate while the server responds with X.509, or both can use ITS certificates. This flexibility allows mixed deployments where legacy systems and modern ITS systems coexist. The CertificateEntry structure now has a case for 1609Dot2 containing cert_data, the opaque ITS certificate bytes.

When a server receives a Client Hello containing these extensions, it selects the most preferred certificate type that both peers support and echoes its choice back in the EncryptedExtensions message. If the server supports none of the proposed types, it terminates with an unsupported_certificate alert.
sections.eli5: Both the client and server say what kind of ID they will show: maybe they both show vehicle IDs, or one shows a vehicle ID and one shows a regular ID. They negotiate which kind to use like picking a language both understand.

sections.title: The CertificateVerify Message for ITS Certificates
sections.content:
When an ITS certificate is used, the CertificateVerify message format changes. Instead of a traditional signature, it becomes an Ieee1609Dot2Data structure of type signed, encoded with Canonical Octet Encoding Rules (OER). This signed data contains:

  • payload with an extDataHash, the SHA-256 hash of the handshake data being signed (identical to standard TLS).
  • headerInfo.psid indicating the application activity the certificate authorizes.
  • headerInfo.generationTime, the time the structure was created.
  • headerInfo.pduFunctionalType set to tlsHandshake (value 1) to disambiguate this use from direct message signing.

The certificate's appPermissions field must permit signing of PDUs with the PSID in the HeaderInfo. If the application specification for that PSID requires SSP (Service Specific Permissions) for tlsHandshake, the SSP must also be present. All other headerInfo fields are omitted.
sections.eli5: When signing the handshake, a vehicle uses its own signature format instead of the regular one. The signature includes the vehicle ID (PSID) and says what it is signing (a TLS handshake), so the same signature cannot be reused for something else.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Certificate lifetime differs between ITS and X.509: ITS certificates are typically short-lived. Implementations accepting ITS certificates MUST check the expiry time and SHOULD terminate a session if a received ITS certificate in the handshake is expired.

Cryptographic strength uses Elliptic Curve Cryptography with 256-bit keys or longer, providing at least 128 bits of security. Implementations SHOULD require that X.509 certificates mixed with ITS certificates also meet this strength threshold.

PSID and pduFunctionalType prevent signature replay: an ITS certificate may be used to sign direct application messages or TLS handshakes. The pduFunctionalType field declares the intent. If absent, the message is for direct application use and MUST NOT be treated as a CertificateVerify. This prevents an attacker from taking a signature meant for one purpose and replaying it in another.

Privacy in vehicular networks is addressed through pseudonym certificates: V2V messages are signed using ITS pseudonym certificates that do not reveal the vehicle's identity, minimizing personal data leakage.
sections.eli5: Vehicle IDs can expire quickly, so both sides must check the date. Vehicles use very strong math to sign. The signature always says what it is for (a secure handshake) so a bad person cannot reuse it for something else.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content:
RFC 8902 is an Experimental protocol. Value 3 was already reserved by IANA for "1609Dot2" and this RFC now provides the official specification for its use in TLS 1.3. The certificate type extension mechanism is designed so that implementations not supporting ITS certificates will recognize the new type and either select a supported alternative or terminate the connection, ensuring segregation between standard TLS and ITS-aware implementations.

ITS certificate use is widespread in vehicular deployments: EU C-ITS systems operate under a certificate policy enabling root CAs across the system, the US USDOT regulation (though not yet in full effect as of publication) requires V2X including ITS certificates, and production deployments in Cadillac vehicles, New York and Tampa traffic systems, and Australian field trials validate the practical use of the extension.
sections.eli5: This is an experimental way to do things that is working in real vehicles on the road today. Different secure-connection systems can choose to understand vehicle IDs or not, without getting confused.
